A ninety-year perspective, Review of Financial Studies","year":1988},{"cite":"Ogden (1990) Turn-of-month evaluations of liquid profits and stock returns: a common explanation for the monthly and January effects, Journal of Finance","year":1990},{"cite":"McConnell, Xu (2008) Equity returns at the turn of the month, Financial Analysts Journal","year":2008},{"cite":"Etula, Rinne, Suominen, Vaittinen (2020) Dash for cash: monthly market impact of institutional liquidity needs, Review of Financial Studies","year":2020}],"signal":{"description":"Instruments: SPY (equity sleeve) and IEF (bond sleeve). Execution: the target of trading day d is decided after the close of the previous trading day d-1 and traded at the open of d. Start: the first full month after both SPY and IEF have prices (IEF starts in mid 2002); before that the strategy holds nothing and is not evaluated. They pay the price impact knowingly or unknowingly because tracking their policy portfolio, governance and benefit cash needs matter more to them than a few basis points of execution cost per month.","why":"Pension funds, balanced funds, target-date funds and other fixed-weight stock/bond mandates rebalance on a calendar schedule, much of it in the last week of the month (benefit payments and month-end valuation). These are large, price-insensitive orders concentrated in a few days, so they create temporary price pressure on the equity/bond spread (Harvey, Mazzoleni, Melone document roughly -17 bp next-day equity return per one-standard-deviation calendar rebalancing signal on S&P 500 and 10y Treasury futures). The strategy takes the other side in advance: it holds the spread the rebalancers will push, and closes at the month-end close when their flow is done.","why_not_arbitraged":"The flow is enormous (trillions in fixed-weight mandates) relative to the risk capital willing to pre-position against it for a few days; the per-month edge is small compared with the spread's volatility, so a front-runner bears real risk for a modest Sharpe. Rebalancers cannot easily change behaviour: schedules are written into investment policy statements and are slow to change, and switching to threshold or smoothed rebalancing has its own costs and committee overhead."},"notes":"Gap from prior_studies: calendar and flow effects. This card is a different mechanism: an asset-allocation rebalancing flow whose sign is set by month-to-date relative performance, traded as a dollar-neutral spread that is short equities about as often as long, and it is flat during the first days of the month (the turn-of-month inflow window). If the Chair nevertheless counts it in turn-of-month-flows, that is acceptable. Not short-term reversal as in studies 5-7: the signal is a month-to-date (about 15 trading days) cross-asset drift, timed to the month-end calendar, and the placebo-window criterion tests exactly that distinction. Costs: two very liquid ETFs, about 24 round trips of gross 1.0 per year. Exposure: gross 1.0 for about 5 of 21 trading days, mean gross exposure about 0.24 (above the 0.20 minimum for the primary; window_days 3 and 4 are below it and are only robustness neighbors). The reference is a 2025 working paper, outside dev, so no publication-decay split is possible in dev; the holdout (2021-2026) is mostly pre-publication. Calendar: XNYS trading days. For each calendar month m let L be the last trading day of m and K = window_days. The window is the last K trading days of month m (L-K+1 .. L). and static-weight investors who keep the same equity share regardless of the risk they are carrying, thereby holding the most variance when its compensation is lowest. The premium is slow to adjust because expected-return beliefs move more slowly than realized volatility.","why":"Equity volatility is highly persistent at horizons of weeks, but the equity premium does not rise in proportion to it: when short-term realized volatility jumps above its long-run level, expected returns per unit of risk (mean/variance) are low, and when volatility is calm they are high (Moreira and Muir 2017; Fleming, Kirby and Ostdiek 2001). The threshold is the natural one (short-run vol equal to its own long-run level, computed point-in-time), not tuned. Binary switching rather than continuous 1/variance scaling is chosen so that the strategy has discrete position entries (expected several regime switches per year, i.e. well over 100 entries and over 36 trading decision dates), and no leverage is needed. Cederburg et al. (2020) is cited as the main counter-evidence: volatility management does not improve Sharpe out of sample for many factors, although the market factor is among the better cases; the literature prior (+20 trials) is accepted. Known risk: in the dev period stock-bond correlation is mostly negative, so IEF tends to rally in the stressed state; the second mechanism criterion is there to separate that from the volatility-timing effect. Costs: SPY and IEF are among the most liquid ETFs, a few switches per year.","references":[{"cite":"Moreira, Muir (2017) Volatility-Managed Portfolios, Journal of Finance","year":2017},{"cite":"Fleming, Kirby, Ostdiek (2001) The Economic Value of Volatility Timing, Journal of Finance","year":2001},{"cite":"Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang, Yan (2020) On the performance of volatility-managed portfolios, Journal of Financial Economics","year":2020}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs: daily total returns of SPY and IEF from sharadar_sfp. Daily close-to-close total return of day d is r_d = (1 + ret_co_d) * (1 + ret_oc_d) - 1, where ret_co_d is previous close to open of d and ret_oc_d is open to close of d. Decision dates: the last trading day of each calendar week (XNYS calendar), after its close t, using only data up to and including that close. On each decision date compute sigma_short = sample standard deviation of SPY daily log total returns over the last short_window_days trading days ending at t, and sigma_long = the same over the last long_window_days trading days ending at t (days without a SPY bar, e.g. vendor-error days dropped by the loader, are simply skipped; the window then extends back to collect the required number of valid returns). Limitation: tradability of t+1 is not known at t, so if only one leg is tradable the engine may fill that leg alone (e.g. sell SPY, IEF bought at the next tradable open), i.e. a short cash interval instead of keeping old holdings. {"files":["strategy/strategy.py","strategy/test_strategy.py"],"summary":"S1: AV = dv(d)/median(dv rows d-63..d-1), NaN if <40 valid days (valid = finite and >0); full stock history used, also before universe entry. S2: event = AVn>=av_threshold and AVn = max of AVn over calendar rows d-21..d+21 (NaN skipped); rows with an incomplete forward window are never events, and at decision t only rows <= t-21 are read. S3: D1 = Monday of the holding week, D5 = D1+4; announcer = event with date in [D1-364-tol, D5-364+tol] AND in [D1-101, D5-81] (counts via cumsum over date->row searchsorted). S4: eligible = member and tradable[t] at the decision row, and defined AVn on >=80% of trading rows with date in (t-380, t]. S5: L = min(0.5, 0.05*N_long), long L/N_long each, other eligible stocks short L/N_short each; flat (zeros) if N_long=0 (also if N_short=0, never in LIQ-500). Non-decision rows NaN; decision rows are full targets (zeros elsewhere). APPROXIMATIONS: last trading day of the week is not knowable PIT; decision rows = Fridays by weekday arithmetic (holidays ignored). If a week has no Friday row (Good Friday, Fri holiday, closures), the first trading row of the next week is a catch-up decision for that current week (D1 = its Monday, trades one day late) instead of skipping the week. 'Trading days' for the median, the +-21 max and the 80% rule are XNYS calendar rows. 'Tradable at the decision close' = tradable[t] (tradable[t+1] is unknown). Payroll and retirement contributions and reinvested coupons and dividends buy equities at the month turn whatever the price. Institutions that sell before month end to raise cash sell at depressed prices and buy back at the turn (Etula et al. estimate their timing loss in the tens of billions of dollars a year). They do it because their payment schedules are fixed by contracts and mandates, not chosen for returns.","why":"The equity market premium is not spread evenly over the month. Payments in the US are standardized around the turn of the calendar month (wages, pension and 401k contributions, coupons, dividends), so cash that must go into equities arrives in bulk in the last day and first days of each month. In the days just before, institutions sell equities to meet month-end cash needs. Price-insensitive buying in the turn-of-month window lifts the market (Ogden 1990; Etula, Rinne, Suominen, Vaittinen 2020). McConnell and Xu (2008) report that over 1926-2005 the US market premium was earned on average almost only in the window from the last trading day to the third trading day of the new month. A dollar-neutral book that is long high-beta and short low-beta stocks has a net market beta near one. Held only inside the window, it collects the window's market premium against a cash benchmark. It does not hold equity beta during the rest of the month, when the premium is claimed to be near zero. Because the book does not switch between SPY and IEF, it avoids the handicap that killed H-0001 (K-0005). Rank-based legs give hundreds of position entries per month, and the claim becomes a cross-sectional event that the judge can test against time-shifted placebos.","why_not_arbitraged":"Collecting the premium means carrying full market risk for a few days every month for a few tenths of a percent. That is a small reward per unit of risk, and it does not scale with leverage for capital that pays for drawdowns. Desks that provide this liquidity are balance-sheet constrained exactly at month and quarter ends. The flow is mandated, so it does not shrink when the premium becomes known."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"After the close of the third-to-last XNYS trading day of a month, a stock in the liq_n universe is in the top quintile (side +1) or bottom quintile (side -1) of trailing 252-day beta to the equal-weighted universe return. Mechanism claim: over the 5 trading days from the next open (the second-to-last trading day) to the close of the third trading day of the new month, high-beta stocks beat the cross-sectional mean and low-beta stocks lag it, by more than the same beta ranking does in time-shifted (non-window) placebo dates.","horizons":[1,3,5,10],"primary_horizon_days":5},"notes":"Brief fit: holding 5 trading days, US single stocks, cross-sectional LIQ-500, mechanism test declared. Family reuse: this is the same economic mechanism as H-0001 (turn-of-month flows), so it is filed under turn-of-month-flows on purpose and adds to that family's trial count. Why it is not a near-copy of H-0001: H-0001 switched the whole book between SPY and IEF and was benchmarked against 60/40. They trade at prices that have not yet absorbed the surprise and lose the subsequent drift.","why":"Post-earnings-announcement drift (Bernard and Thomas 1989): prices under-react to the information in a quarterly earnings surprise, because investors anchor on the previous level of earnings and do not fully see how a year-over-year change carries into later quarters.
